summary: A revision of the Data Transfer Protocol from RFC 171, written by the file transfer committee. It changes sequence number sizes, clarifies modes available messages and code assignments, then restates the whole protocol. It was updated by RFC 310 and replaced by RFC 354.

eli5.summary: The rules for how to chop up and send a stream of data between computers were improved and rewritten in one place.

questions: what is the data transfer protocol
what are the three dtp transfer modes
subtitle: A common protocol for breaking data into chunks and labeling them for transport across the ARPANET.

tldr.problem: Different ARPANET applications (file transfer, remote job entry, email) all needed to send data, but had no common way to split it into logical blocks and mark them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 264 defines seven transaction types: three data and control transfer modes (indefinite stream, transparent block, count-based), plus messages for handshake, separators, error reports, aborts, and no-ops.
tldr.outcome: This RFC was superseded by RFC 354 in 1972. It also updates RFC 114 and is updated by RFC 310.

facts.label: Descriptor field
facts.value: 72 bits (9 bytes) for info count, sequence number, and filler count

facts.label: Sequence number field
facts.value: 16 bits in error and separator transactions

today: RFC 264 was replaced by RFC 354 in 1972. It is primarily of historical interest, as the ARPANET evolved to use simpler transmission protocols.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 264 revises and restates the Data Transfer Protocol (DTP) from RFC 171, improving it based on feedback from the ARPANET community. The RFC provides a common way for applications like file transfer, remote job entry, network mail, and terminal communication to handle data transfer. DTP operates at a level below applications, separating messages into logical blocks called transactions.
sections.eli5: DTP is a common delivery system that different mail, file, and job programs can all use, so they do not have to invent their own ways to send data.

sections.title: Three Transfer Modes
sections.content: DTP supports three ways to split messages into transactions. The indefinite bit stream mode sends data until the connection closes, useful for terminal communication. Transparent block mode ends each transaction when it sees a DLE (Data Link Escape) followed by ETX, with DLE bytes doubled to avoid false endings. Descriptor and counts mode begins each transaction with a 72-bit header containing the byte count and a sequence number, useful for most host-to-host transfers. Applications can mix modes on the same connection.
sections.eli5: There are three ways to mark where one piece ends and the next begins: wait for the connection to close, watch for a special escape signal, or count bytes at the start of each chunk.

sections.title: Transaction Types and Control Messages
sections.content: Each transaction starts with an 8-bit type byte (hex B0 through BF). Types B0, B1, B2 are data modes; B8, B9, BA are their control equivalents. Type B3 is a modes-available handshake; B4 marks file/group/record/unit boundaries with a sequence number; B5 carries error codes; B6 signals abort operations; B7 is a no-op filler. Sequence numbers help detect missing transactions and errors, though implementations may disable them.
sections.eli5: Each chunk has a label that says what kind it is, with special labels for breaking points, errors, and stopping the flow.

sections.title: Connection and Error Handling
sections.content: After a full-duplex connection opens, the first transaction should be type B3 announcing which receive modes are available, allowing the sender to choose one both sides can handle. DTP itself does not define error recovery; that is left to the applications protocol using it. The protocol emphasizes flexibility and implementation freedom, allowing DTP to be embedded in an application, used as a library, or implemented as macros.
sections.eli5: When two computers connect, they first say what delivery styles each understands. If something goes wrong, the application decides what to do about it, not DTP.
